senses.gloss:
kṣetra
(‘field’)
------------------------------------------
Though this word is used in a general sense for an agricultural field, in a more technical sense, it stands for the body since it is through this body that the fruits of karma—good or bad—are reaped (vide Bhagavadgītā 13.1). Later, the same work includes the five elements, egoism, intellect, the ten sense-organs and their objects also under the purview of this term (ibid 13.5 and 6).
Another meaning of the word is ‘a place of पिल्ग्रिमगे’.
In Hindu अस्त्रोलोग्य्, the twelve signs of the zodiac are considered as the kṣetras of the seven प्लनेत्स्. For instance, Ravi (Sun) has Siṁha (Leo) as his क्षेत्र. This helps in estimating the effects of these प्लनेत्स्.

kṣetrajña
(‘one who knows the क्षेत्र’)
------------------------------------------
If the human body is the क्षेत्र or the field (since the human being reaps the results of his karmas through it) then the क्षेत्रज्ञ is the one who resides in it and ‘knows’ it, experiences it and controls it. This is, of course, the jīvātman (the individual सोउल्).
However, the Lord श्रीकृष्ण says in the Bhagavadgītā (13.2) that he too is क्षेत्रज्ञ in all the bodies. This statement can be interpreted from two different standpoints. From the standpoint of advaita, all the jīvātmans or the jīvas are only appearances or reflections of the परमात्मन्. Hence all the jīvas in all the kṣetras or bodies are the Lord Himself.
The भक्ति schools however, which advocate द्वैत or dualism, declare that behind or inside all the jīvas in all the kṣetras, is the one Supreme Lord, ईश्वर as the अन्तर्यामिन्, the inner Self and controller. The Antaryāmi Brāhmaṇa of the Mādhyandina recension of the Bṛhadā-raṇyaka Upaniṣad supports this view (3.7.22).

Kṣetrapāla
(‘guardian of the site’)
------------------------------------------
Among the subsidiary deities in the temples of शिव, the क्षेत्रपाल occupies an important place. He is the chief guardian of the temple. His image is usually naked, with protruding eyes, sharp fangs in the mouth and dishevelled hair. Snakes are his ornaments. He is shown with two or four or even six hands carrying a sword, a bell, a trident, a noose, a skull-cup and fire.
He may have three aspects according to the three guṇas, सत्त्व, रजस् and तमस्. He stands on a lotus and is accompanied by a dog. He is worshipped first before commencing the regular service of the day.
He seems to be an aspect of भैरव.
Kṣetrapāla can also be an independent deity with his own shrine, usually set up in the north-eastern corner of the village or town. This shrine should not face east.

Kṣemaṅkarī
(‘one who brings about the welfare [of beings]’)
------------------------------------------
Worship of God as the Divine मोथेर् is a very old tradition in हिन्दुइस्म्. Most of the Hindu goddesses are facets of पार्वती, the spouse of शिव.
One of the nine aspects of दुर्गा (Navadurgās) is called ‘Kṣemaṅkarī’. She is shown with four arms of which three are carrying त्रिशूल (trident), kamala (lotus) and pānapātra (drinking bowl). The fourth is exhibiting the varadamudrā.
